transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Reeves (CTO, LynxCorp), Priya Singh (Lead ML Eng), Sam Ortiz (SRE)

Summary (auto): quick discovery on dedicated GPU reservations, isolation, burst strategy, scale expectations; security and compliance flagged; agreed to pricing + benchmark next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for making time, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'll hand off to Ravi for a quick intro of our dedicated offering but first can we do quick intros?
[00:08] Jordan Reeves: yeah Jordan, CTO at LynxCorp, today we'll focus on inference for our document classification and chat assistant, mostly latency sensitive for customer-facing flows.
[00:13] Priya Singh: Priya, lead ML, we own the model stack and ops, we've been running on cloud vms with a mix of GPUs but hitting noisy neighbor noise.
[00:19] Sam Ortiz: Sam, SRE, we're evaluating options for isolation and predictable cost.
[00:24] Ravi Patel: thanks, quick flag, we'll cover reserved pools, burst capacity, autoscaling policies, and security (VPC/KMS/SAML). feel free to stop.

[00:45] Maya Chen: Jordan, can you walk through current infra? what are your request patterns, p95/p99 targets, concurrency?
[00:52] Jordan Reeves: sure, right now baseline is 300 rps for classification during peak, bursts can go to 1.2k rps for a few minutes. target p95 of 150ms and p99 under 500ms for the chat bot, classification can be a bit looser. we want isolation because customers demand data separation.
[01:10] Priya Singh: models are a mix, two LLMs for chat (13B and a quantized 7B for scoping) and a custom encoder for embeddings. we've been experimenting with 4-bit quantization; latency is okay but throughput is inconsistent because of shared hosts.
[01:29] Ravi Patel: makes sense. dedicated solves noisy neighbor by reserving GPU pools. you can pin model versions, configure autoscale, and set burst capacity to consume unreserved headroom. question: how important is predictable throughput vs cost optimization?
[01:42] Jordan Reeves: predictable throughput is top priority for us, cost is second but still important. we have compliance requirements too - SOC2 and need KMS integration.
[01:51] Maya Chen: noted. on compliance we have SOC2 docs and KMS/HSM options for private deployments, and for Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS for secrets and support audit logs.

[02:10] Sam Ortiz: on network, we need VPC peering or private link, no public egress for inference traffic. how does Redwood handle private networking?
[02:16] Ravi Patel: for Dedicated we offer VPC connectivity and optional private control plane. you can choose a VPC-only private endpoint and restrict egress. for Private deployments you can go fully customer-managed.
[02:29] Priya Singh: what about bursts? our traffic pattern spikes 3-4x a few minutes a day. we don't want to pay for idle reserved GPUs but also can't risk cold starts.
[02:37] Ravi Patel: two mechanisms: reserved capacity for baseline, and burst capacity that can use shared ledger or spare pool within the same region. you can set autoscale thresholds and a warm pool size to reduce cold start latency. there is an additional per-minute burst charge but it's cheaper than over-provisioning reserved.
[02:57] Jordan Reeves: can bursts be limited to certain models or routes? we want low-cost models to scale out first.
[03:03] Ravi Patel: yes, routing policies let you prefer cheaper model variants for burst, or route by route. also you can set fallbacks so if a primary model is at capacity a lighter quantized variant handles traffic.
[03:15] Priya Singh: how does the runtime handle KV cache and prefix caching for chat? we rely on long contexts for customers.
[03:21] Ravi Patel: we support KV cache management and prefix caching at the runtime; for Dedicated pools you can size cache memory per node. caching reduces token cost and latency but requires sticky routing to maintain cache locality.
[03:34] Sam Ortiz: sticky routing is fine, but that creates imbalanced load sometimes. how do you mitigate that?
[03:38] Ravi Patel: we do dynamic rebalancing and batch padding strategies, plus you can set a small shared cache for hot prefixes across the pool. there are knobs in the console for batch size limits and cache eviction policies.
[03:53] Jordan Reeves: curious about throughput expectations: for our 13B model, what's throughput on an A100-style 80GB or equivalent?
[04:00] Ravi Patel: rough ballpark: for a 13B causal model with opt kernels on A100-ish, you might see 8-12 tokens/ms depending on sequence length and batching. real numbers vary; we recommend running a benchmark with your model and typical sequences.
[04:15] Priya Singh: we'll definitely want to benchmark. can Redwood run benchmarks on our dataset?
[04:19] Maya Chen: yes, Ravi and I can coordinate a benchmark run, we'll need a sample payload and expected concurrency; we usually run a 24-hour soak to capture tails.
[04:29] Jordan Reeves: timeline: we're aiming for a pilot in Q2, production end of Q3 if things go well. compliance review will be parallel.
[04:37] Maya Chen: good, that aligns with typical cycles. any deal-breakers on your side?
[04:41] Priya Singh: encryption at rest and separation of logs is mandatory; also need SSO integration for our devs.
[04:47] Ravi Patel: we have SAML SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. logs can be routed to customer SIEM and you can opt to disable certain telemetry.
[04:58] Sam Ortiz: on billing, do you do monthly reserved commitment for Dedicated? how flexible is resizing?
[05:03] Maya Chen: Dedicated is typically reserved monthly or annual commitments. resizing mid-term is possible but depends on availability; we offer burst headroom to cover short-term spikes.
[05:12] Jordan Reeves: what's the minimum commitment?
[05:14] Maya Chen: minimum depends on region and configuration but commonly starts around 4-8 GPUs equivalent for small pilots; for enterprise deals we model committed throughput. we'll send a sizing worksheet.
[05:25] Priya Singh: what about model compatibility - do you support custom kernels or only our model weights?
[05:30] Ravi Patel: we take model weights and support common frameworks and tokenizers, we handle kernel selection in the runtime. if you have custom ops we can discuss a path but it's more complex.
[05:41] Jordan Reeves: are there any limitations with quantization? our 4-bit experiments gave good perf but some regressions on quality.
[05:47] Ravi Patel: quantization tradeoffs are model-specific. Redwood offers quantization profiles and we can run A/B evals to check regression. Redwood Optimize suggests profiles by workload.
[05:58] Priya Singh: can we pin some routes to a non-quantized model for critical flows?
[06:02] Ravi Patel: absolutely, route-level pinning is supported; canary rollout and A/B with automatic rollback on quality regression are available.
[06:12] Jordan Reeves: on security docs you mentioned SOC2, can we get the cert and the network diagram?
[06:16] Maya Chen: yes we'll share SOC2 report summary and a redacted network diagram; for full access we have an NDA process.
[06:24] Sam Ortiz: any public case studies in regulated industries?
[06:27] Maya Chen: we have a couple of finance and healthcare customers on Dedicated and Private, will include anonymized references.
[06:34] Priya Singh: about SLA - what latency guarantees do you offer for Dedicated?
[06:38] Ravi Patel: dedicated pools have latency SLOs based on instance type and model class; specific p99 targets are in the SLA; for enterprise we can negotiate strict targets with penalties.
[06:50] Jordan Reeves: ok good. next steps recap at high level?
[06:53] Maya Chen: we'll send pricing/sizing spreadsheet, SOC2 and network diagram, and propose a benchmark run. Ravi will draft test plan and we'll sync next week to kick off.
[07:03] Priya Singh: I'll prepare sample traces and a representative payload for the benchmark.
[07:08] Sam Ortiz: I'll follow up on networking contacts for the VPC peering.

[07:20] Jordan Reeves: a couple of quick technical details before we wrap: how do updates/rollouts work to avoid downtime? we need zero-downtime deploys for models.
[07:28] Ravi Patel: we support canary rollouts with traffic mirroring and automatic fallback to previous model if error rates or latency degrade. KV cache warmup can be configured; you can also set rolling restarts across nodes to avoid full pool disruption.
[07:41] Priya Singh: and monitoring hooks? we need token-level cost breakdown and latency traces.
[07:45] Maya Chen: Redwood Console has per-route dashboards, token-level cost, traces, and error analysis. we also expose tracing hooks and webhooks for alerts.

[07:56] Jordan Reeves: any integration work required from our side for KMS?
[08:00] Ravi Patel: typically a KMS role and key policy plus network connectivity; we'll provide an integration doc.

[08:10] Maya Chen: cool, thanks everyone. we'll send the artifacts and action items. anything else?
[08:14] Priya Singh: no, thanks.
[08:15] Jordan Reeves: thanks all.

[08:25] End of recording.

Notes: transcription contains some imperfect names and timings; electrical crosstalk briefly at 00:45.

Recap / Agreed next steps:
- Redwood to send pricing & sizing worksheet and SOC2 + network diagrams (Maya)
- Redwood to schedule benchmark and provide test plan (Ravi)
- LynxCorp to provide sample traces and concurrency targets (Priya/Jordan)
- Schedule 60-min benchmark kickoff next week
